The problem is an instance of exact-weight syndrome decoding: the 15 \(\times\) 400 matrix whose columns are the given vectors over \(\mathbb{Z}/418\mathbb{Z}\) is a parity-check matrix, and a weight-14 error vector must be recovered from the displayed syndrome. Equivalently one must locate a 14-element subset of columns that sum to the syndrome coordinate-wise.

The 15 standard-basis vectors appear among the columns (at the easily identified indices 81, 149, 161, 172, 181, 195, 222, 239, 271, 275, 297, 327, 333, 394, 395). Their presence is consistent with a systematic representation \(H=[I|-G]\), but it does not yield an immediate solution: the syndrome is far from any 0-1 vector of weight 14, so the unknown support cannot consist solely of those identity columns. Exhaustive enumeration of the complementary low-weight cases (error weight 1 or 2 on the identity part) likewise produces no match.

A direct search over all \(\binom{400}{14}\) subsets is impossible by hand, as are the natural meet-in-the-middle and dynamic-programming recurrences (the latter already requires a state space of size \(\Theta(14\cdot418^{15})\)). Modular projections (modulo 2, 11 or 19) and successive closest-vector heuristics likewise fail to isolate a unique candidate that satisfies all 15 coordinates simultaneously.

Consequently the unique increasing 14-tuple cannot be certified without a computer-algebra search that is outside the scope of the present reasoning.
